title: US Dollar Struggles Despite Rising Fed Rate Hike Bets as Yen and Euro Gain
author: James O'Connor
image: /images/news/Dollar Struggles Despite Rising Fed Rate Hike Expectations.webp
excerpt: The US dollar is struggling despite rising expectations of a September Fed rate hike as yen strength, ECB tightening and global inflation risks limit its advantage.
content: The US dollar is struggling to build momentum even as expectations for a Federal Reserve interest-rate hike have increased sharply, highlighting how quickly the currency market can shift when other central banks turn more hawkish at the same time. On Monday, September 7, the dollar traded close to recent lows against a basket of major currencies, with the dollar index around 99.1 after briefly benefiting from a stronger-than-expected US jobs report at the end of last week. Traders were pricing roughly a 57% probability of a quarter-point Federal Reserve rate increase at the September 15-16 meeting. Yet the higher probability of tighter US monetary policy has not translated into a sustained dollar rally.

The immediate explanation is that the US is no longer the only major economy where investors expect interest rates to rise. The Japanese yen has strengthened dramatically as markets increase bets on faster Bank of Japan tightening, while the European Central Bank is also expected to raise rates this week. When several central banks move toward tighter policy at the same time, the interest-rate advantage traditionally enjoyed by the dollar becomes less powerful. Reuters reported Monday that the yen had climbed to a seven-month high, with the dollar falling as low as 154.05 yen before trading around 154.64. The euro also gained to $1.1624, while sterling moved higher to $1.3536.

The US labor market has nevertheless strengthened the case for a Federal Reserve hike. Employers added 162,000 jobs in August, significantly exceeding economists' expectations, while the unemployment rate remained at 4.1%. The report followed hawkish comments from Fed Chair Kevin Warsh, who has emphasized the need for clear evidence that inflation is returning toward the central bank's 2% objective. Financial markets subsequently increased the probability of a September rate move. UBS went further on Monday, changing its forecast from no US policy changes in 2026 to two 25-basis-point rate increases, one in September and another in December.

That would normally provide a strong foundation for the dollar. Higher US rates can increase the return available from dollar-denominated assets, potentially attracting global capital into Treasury securities and other investments. But foreign-exchange markets price relative expectations rather than US monetary policy in isolation. Right now, traders are increasingly focused on what happens in Japan and Europe as well as Washington. The possibility that the Bank of Japan could accelerate tightening has already forced investors to reconsider trades that relied on cheap yen funding, while expectations of further ECB increases are giving the euro an additional source of support.

The yen has become particularly important. The dollar moved through the 155-yen level, a threshold that traders had previously associated with intervention and a potential floor for the Japanese currency. Reuters reported that the break below that level strengthened bullish sentiment toward the yen. Some investors are also unwinding yen-funded carry trades, in which low-cost yen borrowing is used to purchase higher-yielding assets elsewhere. If the yen continues to strengthen, those investors may have to buy yen and sell other currencies, creating another source of pressure on the dollar.

Another factor is the inflationary effect of higher energy prices. The conflict involving the United States and Iran has pushed oil prices higher and increased concerns about inflation across major economies. That could force central banks outside the US to maintain or accelerate restrictive policies. Europe is particularly sensitive because higher energy costs can feed directly into consumer and producer prices. Reuters reported Monday that the ECB is widely expected to raise rates on September 10, while Deutsche Bank now expects another increase in December because of persistent energy-related inflation risks.

That dynamic is weakening one of the dollar's traditional advantages: policy divergence. If the Federal Reserve is tightening while the ECB and Bank of Japan remain accommodative, the dollar can attract significant capital because US assets offer a clear yield premium. But if all three central banks are moving in the same direction, the gap becomes much narrower. Analysts cited by Reuters argued that even a confirmed September Fed hike may not be enough to push the dollar to new cyclical highs because tightening elsewhere is limiting the difference between major economies.

The Federal Reserve itself is not unanimous on the next step. On September 3, Governor Christopher Waller said he would favor keeping rates steady if incoming data confirmed that inflation pressures were continuing to cool. His comments temporarily reduced the market-implied probability of a September hike from 59% to 48%. The subsequent strong employment report reversed some of that move, but it also demonstrated how sensitive the dollar has become to individual economic releases and Fed communication.

This makes Friday's US inflation report particularly important. The August Consumer Price Index will be one of the last major pieces of evidence available to policymakers before the September meeting. A stronger-than-expected CPI reading could increase expectations for a Fed hike and potentially give the dollar a short-term boost. A softer report, meanwhile, could push traders back toward a policy hold and remove some of the support created by the strong payroll numbers. Reuters quoted market strategist Elias Haddad as saying a hot CPI reading could effectively cement a September hike, while a cooler number would leave the dollar vulnerable to a renewed repricing toward a Fed pause.

The currency market is also dealing with concerns that go beyond interest rates. Reuters highlighted worries about rising US government debt and continuing policy uncertainty as additional pressures on the greenback. In normal circumstances, geopolitical stress can strengthen the dollar because investors treat it as a safe-haven currency. But the current environment is more complicated because the same geopolitical tensions are also driving oil prices higher, increasing inflation risks for the United States, Europe and Japan simultaneously. The result is a market in which a classic dollar-positive shock does not necessarily produce a straightforward dollar rally.

For businesses and investors, the dollar's next move could have broad consequences. A stronger dollar can reduce the cost of imported goods and commodities for American consumers while making US exports more expensive abroad. A weaker dollar can have the opposite effect and may provide some support for multinational companies' overseas earnings when converted back into US currency. It also matters for emerging markets, where dollar strength can increase the burden of dollar-denominated debt and affect capital flows.

The September Fed decision will therefore be about more than a quarter-point move. Investors are trying to determine whether the US is entering a renewed tightening cycle or whether a possible hike represents a short-lived response to stronger employment and persistent inflation risks. UBS's revised forecast for two hikes this year suggests some institutions see a more durable shift in Fed policy, but the market remains far from fully convinced.

For now, the dollar's weakness sends a clear message: higher US interest rates alone are no longer enough to guarantee a stronger currency. The yen's comeback, potential ECB tightening, energy-driven inflation and uncertainty over the Fed's next move are all competing for investors' attention. The next major test comes with US inflation data and the September Federal Reserve meeting. Until those events pass, the dollar is likely to remain caught between stronger US rate expectations and an increasingly hawkish global policy backdrop.

Markets will focus on the August US CPI report ahead of the Federal Reserve's September 15-16 meeting. Investors will also monitor the ECB's September 10 decision, Bank of Japan policy signals and the direction of oil prices. A hotter US inflation report could strengthen the case for a Fed hike and temporarily support the dollar, while stronger yen and euro expectations could continue to limit its upside.
